title: The Contract
concept: After this one you can write a deal that holds: both sides say yes to the same clear thing, each gives something back, both are fit to agree, and nothing in it has to be hidden.
bookIdea: Steiner takes four requirements for a valid contract from law and applies them to helping: mutual consent to a clear and specific offer, something given in return (consideration), parties who are able to agree (competency), and an aim that is lawful.
bookSource: Scripts People Live, ch. 20; TA Today, ch. 26

opener.setting: Sunday, 8:40pm, Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B, the kitchen table. Maya has come in from a double shift and got a notebook out of the drawer anyway.

lines.text: “I'm done saying it's fine. Get a pen. We're writing down who does what.”
lines.cue: still in her scrubs, notebook already open

lines.text: “If it isn't written, it doesn't happen. I'm not doing another month like the last one.”
lines.cue: tapping the blank page with the pen

opener.ask: What has to be in a deal before it holds?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: A deal that holds has four things in it. Both sides say yes to the same clear thing. Each side gives something. Both are fit to agree. Nothing in it breaks the law or the lease. Tap the one each line is making sure of.

items.text: “Say it back to me. Your share, into my account, by the 5th of every month. Yes or no?”
items.cue: pen on the page, waiting for him to answer
items.why: She has named the exact thing and asked for a yes to it. Afterwards, both of you can say what was agreed and what counts as done, and that is what a clear yes means.

traps.1: Something each way. It sounds like a swap, but only Sam's side is named. Maya gives nothing in this line, so the exchange is still missing.
traps.2: Above board. Nothing here is hidden, but the line asks Sam to agree to a set term. Whether the term is allowed is a separate question.

items.example:
Allotment association, Saturday.
Chair: “Plot holders pay the water fee by the 1st. Do you agree?”
You: “Agreed. The 1st.”
Treasurer: “Noted.”

items.text: “If I cook on Tuesdays, what comes back from you? A deal where only one of us gives is a favour, and I'm done with favours.”
items.why: She is asking what Sam gives in return. A deal needs something going each way, or one person gives and the other takes.

traps.0: Fit to agree. It sounds like she is checking his state of mind, but nothing in the line is about whether he can understand the deal.
traps.2: A clear yes. She wants a yes in the end, but this line asks what comes back, not whether he agrees to a set term.

items.example:
Language exchange, Wednesday, 6:00pm.
Tutor: “I'll teach you English for an hour. What will you teach me?”
You: “Cooking. I'll bring the food next week.”
Tutor: “Done. Same time Wednesday.”

items.text: “It's one in the morning and you've had four beers. We'll write this tomorrow, when you can say yes and mean it.”
items.why: She is checking that Sam can understand what he is agreeing to. A yes from someone who is drunk or half asleep doesn't count, so she waits.

traps.1: Something each way. The deal does need a swap, but this line says nothing about what each of you gives. Its only concern is whether he can agree tonight.
traps.2: Above board. Nothing here is against the law or the lease. The worry is the state he is in tonight.

items.example:
Car showroom, Saturday, 4:00pm.
Salesman: “Sign today and I'll knock off the delivery fee.”
Buyer: “I've been up since four with my daughter. I'll come back Monday and read it properly.”

items.text: “I'm not writing down anything that breaks the lease. If it has to be hidden from the landlord, it isn't a deal.”
items.why: She is refusing to put anything in the deal that breaks the lease or the law. A deal that depends on hiding something isn't one that holds.

traps.0: A clear yes. The deal does need one, but this line says nothing about spelling out terms. It limits what the terms are allowed to be.
traps.1: Fit to agree. That is about whether Sam can understand the deal. This line is about the deal's content, which is being kept legal.

items.example:
Market stall, Sunday.
Seller: “I can do you a better price if we skip the receipt.”
You: “I'll pay the normal price and take the receipt, thanks.”

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Two sorts. First, build the deal: put each line under the part it covers. Then sort drafts that don't hold.

items.prompt: Build the deal. Tap a line, then the part of the deal it covers.

items.text: “From the 1st, your share goes into my account by the 5th. Yes or no?”
items.why: It names the exact thing and asks for a yes, so both of you can say later what was agreed.

items.text: “A night counts as done when the plates are on the rack and the pans are soaking.”
items.why: It says what finished looks like in terms anyone can see from the doorway. Steiner wants the aim stated as something you can watch happen.

items.text: “You cook Mondays and Wednesdays. I cook Tuesdays and Thursdays.”
items.why: Each person gives something, and each person's share is named, so nobody is left wondering whose turn it is.

items.text: “I'll look over your CV tonight, and you take the bins out until the end of the month.”
items.why: Help goes one way and bins go the other, so neither of you ends up giving more than you get.

items.text: “My cousin is fifteen and staying for the summer, so his mum is part of this deal too.”
items.why: A young person can't agree to a deal on his own, so the adult who answers for him joins in. Steiner says the same of minors.

items.text: “The box room stays as the lease allows: one tenant, and no cash on the side.”
items.why: Nothing in this line has to be hidden from the landlord. A deal that holds stays inside the law and the lease.

items.prompt: These drafts don't hold. Put each one under what is wrong with it.

items.text: “Keep the flat nice, and we'll see how it goes.”
items.why: Nice has no edge. Neither of you could say afterwards what was agreed, which is why Steiner says vague aims can't be contracted.

items.text: “I'll cover your rent this month, and you'll remember it every time you're late with mine.”
items.why: The price, remembering it, is never stated as a term. Sam can't say yes to something he hasn't been told, so the favour hides a bill.

items.text: “I'll lend you my laptop all term. Don't worry, you don't owe me anything.”
items.why: A gift is fine in life. In a deal meant to hold, nothing coming back leaves one person giving and the other taking, which is how a rescue starts.

items.text: “It's one in the morning, you've had four beers, and you said yes to every line. Done.”
items.why: A yes from someone who is drunk doesn't count. Steiner says a deal made in that state is not valid, so it waits for the morning.

items.text: “Sam's friend takes the box room for cash, and the landlord isn't told.”
items.why: The deal depends on hiding something from the landlord. Steiner requires an aim that is lawful, and this one fails it.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Now the book's words for the four. Steiner's names for them are mutual consent, consideration, competency and lawful object.

items.text: “I'll be more responsible about the flat from now on.”
items.cue: said across the kitchen table, pen not yet picked up. Which explanation fits?
options: It is a fair start. A good intention is enough to begin with, and the details can come later.
It fails mutual consent. Neither of you could say afterwards what was agreed, so there is nothing to say yes to. Steiner wants the aim stated as something you can see someone do.
It fails consideration. Sam gives nothing in return, so Maya would be doing a rescue.
items.why: Mutual consent needs a clear offer and a clear yes, in terms you could watch happen. 'More responsible' is the kind of vague aim Steiner says can't be contracted, because neither side can say what they have agreed to.

traps.0: A good intention feels like a start, and it is a kind thing to say. But with nothing anyone can see, the first argument will be about what 'responsible' meant.
traps.2: Consideration is about what comes back. Sam is offering to change himself, so something is on offer. The trouble is that nobody can tell what it is.

items.example:
Running club, Tuesday, 6:30pm.
Member: “I'll try to be more committed.”
Captain: “Which nights, and from when?”
Member: “Tuesdays and Saturdays, from this week.”
Now there is something to say yes to.

items.text: “I'll cook every night this term. You don't have to do anything for it.” Sam says: “Deal.”
items.cue: the notebook is still shut. Which explanation fits?
options: Mutual consent is missing. Sam only said 'Deal', so he hasn't really agreed.
Consideration is missing. Nothing comes back from Sam, so Maya gives and Sam takes. Steiner says that without something in return, helping slides into a rescue.
Competency is missing. Maya is tired after a double shift, so her offer doesn't count.
items.why: The terms are clear and Sam said yes, so consent is there. What is missing is something from Sam. Steiner says the person helped needs to give something back, and when that stops, the helping becomes a rescue.

traps.0: Mutual consent. 'Deal' to a clear offer is a yes. The terms are exact, so consent is present.
traps.2: Competency. Being tired isn't what Steiner means. He means people who can't understand what they are agreeing to, such as someone drunk or a child with no adult in the deal. Maya understands her offer.

items.example:
Neighbours, Sunday morning.
Neighbour: “I'll mow your lawn every week. Don't do anything for it.”
You: “Okay, thanks.”
By July you dread the doorbell, and he is sour about a lawn he never gets thanked for.

debrief.nadia: A deal holds when you could check it on any Tuesday, when both sides give something, when both are in a fit state to say yes, and when nothing in it has to be hidden. Most of the trouble in a flat comes from a yes that was never quite a yes. If one of you isn't sure yet, try it for a few weeks and say yes again.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a contract. Steiner borrows four requirements from contract law: mutual consent, something given in return, parties able to agree, and an aim that is lawful.

reflection.prompt: Is there a deal you are in this week where one of you gives and the other only takes? What could the other side give back?
